newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's CDU agrees on German pensions reform.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's CDU agrees on German pensions reform.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) on Wednesday agreed among themselves a plan to remodel Germany's generous state pensions system without going for a radical overhaul.

Delegates at a mini-party conference gave their backing to a plan broadly based on proposals drawn up by Labour Minister Norbert Bluem which would reduce the value of pensions to 64 percent of net pay by 2030 from 70 percent now.
"The party has taken a good decision on a question which is vital for the future," Kohl said at the end of the day-long meeting.

Kohl said he would now seek to thrash out a common position on pensions with his coalition partners -- Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and above all the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) who have objected to a number of Bluem's proposals.

Kohl said he believed draft legislation should be ready by parliament's summer break and called on party functionaries to promote the pensions reform among voters, saying it would be a vote-winner at next year's general election.

Reform of the pensions system is vital to cope with the "greying" of Germany's 80 million population. Without reforms, the doubling of the number of pensioners by 2030 threatens to put intolerable burdens on the pay-as-you-go scheme.
The pensions shakeup is one element of a complex plan including big tax and health reforms designed to revitalise Germany's social market economy, which is dogged by high unemployment.
Bluem, who has been in Kohl's cabinet since 1983, has had to fight substantial opposition within his own party from critics calling for a more radical overhaul of the system.

But his plan has now survived mostly intact against another scheme for a tax-financed minimum basic pension drawn up by Saxony state premier Kurt Biedenkopf and a proposal by the CDU's youth wing intended to give young Germans a better deal.
"Only the existing pensions system can secure solidarity between the generations," Bluem said.
He added, however, that savings were needed to prevent young people paying unfairly high contributions. Pension charges rose this year to a record 20.3 percent of wages.

Bluem's idea for a tax-financed "family fund" to cover unrelated items borne by contributions was rejected. It will be replaced by a 15 billion mark budget cash injection, which will enable contributions to be cut by one percentage point.
Biedenkopf attacked Bluem's scheme for failing to address record unemployment, which is at a post-war record 4.7 million.

"Above all it won't help reduce unemployment because it won't bring a long-term reduction in labour costs," Biedenkopf told the conference. German occupational insurance costs, at over 40 percent of wages, are among the highest in Europe.

Klaus Escher, chairman of the CDU's youth wing, said the scheme would make a mockery of Bluem's motto "your pension is safe" for people born after 1965. "The young generation won't buy the CDU's pensions policy," he said.
However, only 14 of the 146 delegates voted against the plan based on Bluem's proposals.
FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle welcomed the CDU's decision to drop the family fund, while the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said they were ready to negotiate on pensions.
SPD social policy spokesman Rudolf Dressler said, however, that cutting the pension to 64 percent was unacceptable and would force thousands of old people into poverty.
